Summary
Buddy Rae, a veteran, reflects on his return from Manila to the United States in March 1946, detailing his journey home and the challenges he faced, including poor food and sea sickness. He updates Buddy-Roe on the lives of friends and colleagues, including Fee's family's arrival, Kilduff's plans to open a law office, and Foster's departure for the states. The letter also mentions the difficulty of opening a pub due to a beer shortage and the heat in New York. The tone is nostalgic and informative, with a touch of humor.

--- Page 1 (Beckerman_62a) --- Dear "Buddy-Roe": #1 I realize it has taken me sometime to answer your letter, but from your own experience you know that it takes a little while to get re-adjusted and settled down. I left Manila March 19, 1946, and had a fast trip home, arriving in Frisco on March 28. Was separated at Fort Douglas, Salt Lake City, Utah, April 2. It was a Navy transport on which we returned and the first week was wonderful. He evidently took a short cut and the second week it was rough and stormy all the way home, with about one-half of the passengers sea-sick all the time. The food was very poor and even with six full colonels making a squawk, it improved very little. We were certainly under the iron hand of the Navy. Received a letter sometime ago from Fee and at that time his family had not yet arrived from Australia. He did mention that he talks to his wife on the average of twice a week. I suppose by now they have arrived here and he may have quieted down a little. I can just picture him when he heard them mention that Dorreen was here or anyone else who happened to arrive earlier than his family. Kilduff is apparently planning to open his own law office. He seems to be quite fed up with the Army and all governmental agencies. Gritton has been the Fiscal Director at Camp Robinson, Arkansas, but the post sed to cler part of heard froce that tf June. Lenow stays in Manila Foster should have a pretty good go. I understood Dale was on her way to Manila and ap- parently Farnum had lined up a job for her in the Audit Division. He MEMBER FEDERAL RESERVE SYSTEM MEMBER FEDERAL DEPOSIT INSURANCE CORPORATION --- Page 2 (Beckerman_62b) --- Page 2 - July 25, 1946. and Ruff were the only two old-timers still on duty when I left. You mentioned in your letter that you ran into Bob Hastings in Chicago and that from all indications he had not changed much from his Bostonian ways. When you talked to Bro's Mother did you find out whether he was still in Chicago or had he gone to California? He planned to stay at home for a couple of months and in the event he did not find a job which he considered suitable he was going to leave for the West Coast which seems to be quite a haven for all former Finance Officers. After loafing for about a month I returned to the bank and through vacations, sickness and personnel quitting we have been pretty busy. Received a letter from the post where I was separated, and which is one probably sent to all officers, relative to returning to active duty. I noticed, however, it was all overseas duty and while you might return in the grade held at the time of release you, nevertheless, were subject to rank reduction at any time. I was thinking if you are still as dissatisfied as your letter indicated, it might be an opportunity for you to go back for a year or two, choosing a different theater than the Pacific. From reports I have heard concerning some of the boys in the occupation zones, they seem to be having a pretty nice go of it. All plans for me to open "Pete's Pub" fell by the way side when I arrived home and found such a shortage of even 3.2 beer and you well know that a "Pub" without beer would be a pretty sad place. Sorry to hear your deal on the export-import business fell through, but if you don't return to the Army something just as good may show up. I don't know how it has been in New York, but it has been hotter than hell here the last three weeks. The temperature reached 104 a couple of days and it was pretty rough. Fortunately, the bank is air-conditioned, so we at least get relief during working hours. Of course, like yourself, after spending all that time in the steamy jungles I am more or less immune to it, but it still gets pretty damn hot and uncomfortable. Received a 'phone call from Tulsa, Oklahoma, one Sunday morning from Lough. He apparently was still stiff from the night before and told me he had just finished talking to Billings in St. Louis.
